deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The page continues the worked example from the previous page: an occultation of a star by the Moon, observed at Göttingen. It has two columns, immersion ('Eintritt') and emersion ('Austritt'). The method is the orthographic projection onto the plane through the Earth's centre perpendicular to the star direction (the 'fundamental plane').

Units and constants (from the logs; my interpretation):
- The unit is the arcsecond. The Moon's horizontal parallax is ϖ = 10^3.55854 ≈ 3618″.
- Göttingen's geocentric radius factor is log ρ = 9.99911; on the previous page this log is mislabelled 'sin δ'. Hence P = ρϖ, log P = 3.55765.
- The geocentric latitude is φ ≈ 51°21′ (log cos φ = 9.79562, log sin φ = 9.89261).
- The star's declination is δ ≈ +16°06′ (log sin δ = 9.44356, log cos δ = 9.98258). This makes Aldebaran very likely; that identification is mine.
- The Moon's semidiameter is ϱ ≈ 993.7″ (C.ϱ = 7.00274).
- The relative hourly motion is n ≈ 0.611″/s ≈ 36.7′/h (C.n = 0.21372).
- The direction of relative motion is ζ = 10°11′22″.
- At the epoch Θ = 22h27m6.9s (Paris time) the Moon's centre is at (0, b) with b = 1810.2.

Step 1. Observer's projected coordinates for the assumed hour angle h:
- ξ = P cosφ sin h. Immersion: h = 331°56′20″, log sin h = 9.67248n, log ξ = 3.02575n, ξ ≈ −1060.6. Emersion: h = 347°49′30″, log sin h = 9.32407n, log ξ = 2.67734n, ξ ≈ −475.6.
- η = P sinφ cosδ − P cosφ sinδ cos h, i.e. 2709.2 − 552.7 = 2156.5 (immersion) and 2709.2 − 612.3 = 2096.9 (emersion). Here log(P cosφ sinδ) = 2.79683 and log cos h = 9.94569 / 9.99012.

Step 2. Vector from the Moon's centre at Θ (point 1) to the observer (point 3):
- Components (ξ, η − b), with η − b = 346.3 (log 2.53945) and 286.7 (log 2.45743).
- Direction μ: μ = 161°55′31″ and 148°55′24″, using |cos μ| logs 9.97802 and 9.93272.
- Length q = ξ/cos μ: log q = 3.04773 and 2.74462.

Step 3. Contact condition. The triangle has sides 1→2 = nθ (direction ζ), 1→3 = q (direction μ), and 3→2 = ϱ (direction ζ+90°+ν), as defined on the previous page.
- The component perpendicular to ζ gives cos ν = q sin(ζ−μ)/ϱ.
- ζ−μ = 208°15′51″ / 221°15′58″, with log sin = 9.67535n / 9.81925n.
- So log cos ν = 9.72582n / 9.56661n, giving ν = ±122°8′0″ / ±111°37′56″.
- Gauss takes +ν for immersion and −ν for emersion. This is evident from the next log, 9.52635n = log cos(ζ−μ−111°37′56″).

Step 4. Time of contact. The component along ζ gives nθ = ϱ cos(ζ−μ+ν)/sin(ζ−μ).
- log(ϱ/sin(ζ−μ)) = 3.32191n / 3.17801n.
- log cos(ζ−μ+ν) = 9.93926 / 9.52635n; add C.n = 0.21372.
- Result: θ = −2984.6 s = −49m44.6s, and θ = +828.1 s = +13m48.1s.
- Θ+θ = 21h37m22.3s and 22h40m55.0s (Paris).
- Adding the longitude difference Göttingen−Paris of 30m23.0s gives Göttingen times 22h7m45.3s and 23h11m18.0s.
- The h values are evidently improved iterates of the previous page's trials (327°45′, 329°53′, 353°23′). The hour-angle difference, 15°53′10″, matches the time difference of 63m33s mean ≈ 15°55′ sidereal to about 2′, consistent with iteration.

Step 5. Circumstances of the contact:
- tan M = −ξ/η, giving M = −26°11′56″ / −12°46′55″ (log cos M = 9.95292 / 9.98910). Here 90°−M is the direction of the vertical in the projection.
- r = η/cos M: log r = 3.38083 / 3.33248.
- Altitude a from cos a = r/ϖ (log ϖ = 3.55854). Emersion: a = 53°32′37″. Immersion: 48°23′47″, which is struck out; recomputation gives about 48°22.8′.
- Position angles of the contact point:
  - from the equator, ζ+ν = 132°19′22″ / −101°26′34″;
  - from the ecliptic, ζ+ν−p with p = 9°15′6″, giving 123°4′16″ / −110°41′40″;
  - from the vertex, ζ+ν+M = 106°7′26″ / −114°13′29″.

Step 6 (lower half). Formulas for the limit of the occultation: the place with hour angle h at which the star just grazes the Moon's southern limb, allowing for the Earth's ellipticity (A:B = equatorial diameter : axis). Here η now denotes the Moon's ordinate b at Θ, ψ is the reduced latitude and φ′ the geographic latitude.
- The observer's coordinates are ξ = ϖ cosψ sin h and η_obs = ϖ[(B/A) sinψ cosδ − cosψ sinδ cos h].
- The grazing condition is that the Moon's centre lies ϱ north of the observer, perpendicular to the path: ξ sinζ + (b − η_obs) cosζ = ϱ.
- Put tan M = tanζ/sinδ (formula 1). Then sin h tanζ + sinδ cos h = sinδ cos(M−h)/cos M.
- Put tan N = (A/B) tanδ cos(M−h)/cos M (formula 2). The condition becomes (A/B)(ϱ − b cosζ) cos N/(ϖ cosζ cosδ) = sin(N−ψ) (formula 3).
- Formula 4, tanφ′ = (A/B) tanψ, converts the reduced latitude to the geographic latitude.
- The time follows from nθ = ξ cosζ + (η_obs − b) sinζ. Eliminating η_obs with the graze condition gives θ = ϖ cosψ sin h/(n cosζ) − (ϱ/n) tanζ (formula 5).
- For the northern limb, replace ϱ by −ϱ.
errors: Immersion altitude 48°23′47″ is struck out. My recomputation from log r − log ϖ = −0.17771 gives arccos(0.66419) ≈ 48°22.8′, so the struck value appears to be about 1′ off. This is probably why it was cancelled; no corrected value is written.
No other errors found. All logarithms, angles and time sums I checked agree to within 5-place-table precision: μ, q, ζ−μ, ν, θ, the times, M, the emersion altitude and the position angles.
Sign convention for ν (cos ν leaves ν ambiguous; +ν for immersion, −ν for emersion) is implicit and not stated on the page, but it is used correctly.
Bottom formulas 1–5 verified symbolically by me. Note that η in formula 3 means the Moon's ordinate at Θ, not the observer's η used in the numerical columns (overloaded notation).

results.what: Prediction of immersion/emersion times of a star occultation by the fundamental-plane (orthographic projection) method, with iterative correction of the hour angle and the triangle solution nθ = ϱ cos(ζ−μ+ν)/sin(ζ−μ), cos ν = q sin(ζ−μ)/ϱ.
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange/Lambert projection methods (18th c.); systematized by Bessel (1820s–1840s)

results.what: Position angles of the contact point from the equator, the ecliptic and the vertex, plus the altitude of the star at contact.
results.modern_name: Position angle / vertex angle of occultation contact

results.what: Closed formulas (with auxiliary angles M, N) for the grazing limit curve of an occultation on an ellipsoidal Earth, using reduced latitude ψ and tanφ′ = (A/B) tanψ.
results.modern_name: Northern/southern limit (graze line) of a lunar occultation including Earth's oblateness
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel (Analyse der Finsternisse, 1842) and later ephemeris offices for systematic limit curves

deep.surprise_reason: This is competent, correct computational astronomy. Gauss's command of eclipse and occultation theory is well known, and projection methods predate him. The closed-form graze-limit formulas with ellipticity are a neat unpublished detail, but not a result credited to someone else as a discovery.

checkable.asserts: grazing condition reduces to (B/A)(tan N cosψ − sinψ): equals 0
formula 5: nθ = ξ/cosζ − ϱ tanζ given the graze condition

transcription_corrections: Marginal labels omitted in the transcription: 'ν' beside 122.8.0, 'q' beside 3.04773, 'sin(ζ−μ)' beside 9.67535n, 'cos ν' beside 9.72582n, 'cos(ζ+ν−μ)' beside 9.93926.
Struck '48.23.47' is the immersion altitude; the transcription correctly marks it as deleted.
In formula 3 the symbol after N− is ψ (psi), matching formulas 4–5.
Previous page: '9.99911 sin δ' is actually log ρ (the geocentric radius factor), since P = 3.55854 + 9.99911 − 10 = 3.55765; sin δ is 9.44356.
